title: Waking
hook: the first thought of the day can be a prayer
tomorrow: can you hand over a whole day before it starts?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: pray for them, the living and the dead. That closed the works of mercy. Now, the ordinary day, from its very first minute.

The alarm goes off. A hand finds the phone before the eyes are fully open, and the first thought of the day arrives from someone else: a headline, a group chat, an email that can't wait. By the time feet touch the floor, the day has already picked its mood. The Psalms describe a different first move. In the Douay-Rheims: "O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice." The first word goes out before anything comes in.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE PHONE.` → `SOMEONE ELSE'S FIRST THOUGHT.` → `IN THE MORNING, MY VOICE.`

segments.voice: This part of the path is ordinary holiness, the day itself, and it starts where the day does. The tradition's answer to yesterday's question is simple: let the first thought be a turn toward God. The psalmist plans it like an appointment. In the morning, he says, I will stand before you. Lamentations, written among ruins, says God's mercies are "new every morning." Not leftovers from yesterday. New. So Catholic habit has built small doors into the first minute. Some make the sign of the cross before their feet touch the floor. Some say one word of thanks, the way an abuela might say gracias a Dios before she's even sitting up. Some offer the whole day, which is tomorrow's story. And the Church's own morning prayer begins with a line from the Psalms asking God to open my lips, so my mouth can praise. Notice how physical it all is. The first sound. The light under the curtain. The cold floor. Each can become a bell. Here's one to tell a friend: in the Rule of Saint Benedict, monks rising in the dark open their night prayer with that psalm line, said three times, so the first thing they say is praise. The point isn't a long prayer at dawn. It's who gets the first thought. Everything else can wait one breath.
screen: `IN THE MORNING I WILL STAND BEFORE YOU.` · `NEW EVERY MORNING.` · `A SIGN OF THE CROSS, A THANKS.` · `THE FIRST SOUND IS A BELL.` · then, large: `FIRST THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Listen for one sound around you right now: a fridge humming, a car outside, your own breath. Let it be the bell of a small new morning in the middle of your day. When you've found it, let one first thought follow it, a thanks or a name, or if you pray, the psalm's line: in the morning thou shalt hear my voice.
Waking. The first minute of the day, and the first thought in it, turned toward God.
Your line: first thought. Mercies come new every morning, before the phone does. See you at sunrise.

howItsDone: Catholics often begin the day with the sign of the cross, a short prayer of thanks or a morning offering; the Church's Morning Prayer (Lauds) in the Liturgy of the Hours opens with the psalm verse asking God to open our lips.

chat.says: sleeping at Abuela's to help. first thing she says every morning: gracias a Dios. wrist and all. how??

It means her wrist doesn't hurt much anymore, so she feels thankful.

chat.meaning: The psalm says, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice. A first thought turned to God is a habit chosen before the day starts.

notes: Douay-Rheims Psalm 5:4 ('O Lord, in the morning thou shalt hear my voice') and Lamentations 3:23 ('new every morning') quoted from memory; confirm. Psalm 5:5 ('In the morning I will stand before thee') paraphrased.

'The Church's own morning prayer begins with a line from the Psalms asking God to open my lips': the invitatory of the Liturgy of the Hours (Psalm 51:15 / Douay 50:17), paraphrased because the modern liturgical English is not public domain. Confirm.

'In the Rule of Saint Benedict, monks rising in the dark open their night prayer with that psalm line, said three times': Rule of St. Benedict, ch. 9 ('Domine, labia mea aperies' said three times at the start of the night office). Confirm.
The phone-and-alarm opening is an illustration, not a claim about how many people do it.
Original game: Latin mane (Vulgate Psalm 5:4, 'mane exaudies vocem meam'); confirm.
